title: Rendering and Reconciliation
summary: Reconciliation is the algorithm that turns a new virtual tree into minimal real-DOM operations. Its heuristics — same type updates in place, different type replaces — are exactly why `key` exists and why getting it wrong causes state to land on the wrong row.

slides.markdown:
[Reactivity Models](reactivity-models) covered how frameworks decide *that* something changed. **Reconciliation** is the next step: once you have a new tree describing the UI, how do you turn it into the smallest possible set of real DOM operations?

A naive diff would compare full trees pairwise, which is mathematically expensive — O(n³) for a general tree-diff algorithm. React and similar frameworks instead use a set of pragmatic heuristics that run in O(n) and are right almost all the time, at the cost of being occasionally wrong in ways you have to work around.

The most common way this topic shows up in interviews isn't "explain the algorithm" — it's a debugging exercise: "why did this component's internal state end up attached to the wrong row after a list reorder." That bug, and the fix (`key`), is the practical payoff of understanding reconciliation.

slides.sectionTitle: From element tree to DOM operations
slides.markdown:
Reconciliation takes two inputs — the previous virtual tree and the new one — and produces a list of real DOM instructions: insert this node, remove that one, update this attribute, move this node to a new position.

It operates **recursively, level by level**: at each pair of corresponding nodes, it asks one question first — are these the same *type* of thing? — before it even looks at their contents. That single question is the heuristic the whole algorithm is built on, and it's the subject of the next slide.

The reason this matters practically: reconciliation isn't just an implementation detail you can ignore. Its heuristics directly determine whether a component instance (and everything it's holding in its own internal state) is **reused** across a re-render or **thrown away and recreated** — which is observable behavior, not just a performance concern.

slides.sectionTitle: Same type updates in place, different type replaces
slides.markdown:
The core heuristic, applied at every node pair during the diff:

- **Same element type** (`<div>` → `<div>`, or `MyComponent` → `MyComponent`) → the framework **updates the existing DOM node/component instance in place**. Only the changed attributes or children get patched; the underlying instance — and any internal state it holds — survives.
- **Different element type** (`<div>` → `<span>`, or `ComponentA` → `ComponentB`) → the framework **tears down the old subtree entirely and builds a new one from scratch**. The old DOM nodes are removed, the old component instance is unmounted (running any cleanup), and a brand-new instance is mounted in its place.

This is why swapping between two visually-similar components conditionally (`{isEditing ? <EditForm /> : <ViewForm />}`) resets any internal state either one was holding — they're different types, so the framework never considers reusing one instance for the other, no matter how similar their rendered output looks.

slides.subTitle: Stable identity across re-renders
slides.markdown:
Reconciling a list is the same same-type-vs-different-type heuristic applied position by position — **unless** you give the framework something better to match on: a `key`.

Without a `key`, the framework compares the old list and new list **by index**: old position 0 vs new position 0, old position 1 vs new position 1. If the list simply grew or shrank at the end, that's fine. If an item was **inserted at the front** or the list was **reordered**, index-based comparison sees the wrong pairs as "the same node updated" — because it never actually knows an item's *identity*, only its position.

A `key` gives every item a stable identity independent of position, so the framework can correctly recognize "item with key='42' moved from index 2 to index 0" as a **move**, not as "the item currently at index 0 changed its content to whatever item 42 contains." Get the key right and reordering just moves DOM nodes; get it wrong and the framework quietly re-associates the wrong internal state with the wrong visible row.

slides.subTitle: It works — until the list changes order
slides.markdown:
```jsx
{todos.map((todo, index) => (
  <TodoRow key={index} todo={todo} />   // looks fine, is a trap
))}
```

Using the array index as `key` compiles, renders correctly on first paint, and passes a casual code review — because for a **static, never-reordered, never-filtered** list, index and identity happen to be the same thing. The moment the list can insert, delete, filter, or reorder, they diverge: deleting item 0 shifts every subsequent item's index down by one, so the framework sees "item at index 1 changed its content" for every row after the deletion, when actually no row's *data* changed at all — only its position did.

The visible symptom is exactly the "state on the wrong row" bug: if `TodoRow` holds local state (an expanded/collapsed flag, an in-progress edit), that state stays attached to the **index**, not the todo, so after a deletion the wrong row appears expanded or mid-edit. The fix is to key by something stable and unique to the data itself — a database id, never the array position.

slides.sectionTitle: A list re-render bug from missing keys, and the fix

slides.markdown:
| Framework | Reconciliation strategy |
|---|---|
| **React** | virtual-DOM diff with the type/key heuristics described in this topic |
| **Vue 3** | virtual-DOM diff, plus compiler-generated "patch flags" that mark which parts of a template are dynamic, so static parts skip diffing entirely |
| **Svelte** | no runtime reconciliation at all — the compiler determines at build time exactly which DOM operations a given state change requires, and emits that code directly |

Vue's patch flags are worth naming specifically: because the template compiler knows at build time which attributes are ever dynamic, it can skip diffing static children entirely rather than discovering at runtime that they never change — a middle ground between React's fully runtime diff and Svelte's fully compile-time approach.

slides.sectionTitle: Reconciliation is O(n), not the general O(n³)
slides.markdown:
A general tree-diff algorithm that finds the true minimal edit distance between two arbitrary trees is O(n³) in the number of nodes — far too slow to run on every keystroke. React's reconciliation gets this down to **O(n)** by giving up generality for two assumptions that are true almost all the time in real UI:

- **Elements of different types produce substantially different trees.** So the algorithm never tries to find a partial match between a `<div>` subtree and a `<span>` subtree — it just replaces, which is a much cheaper operation than searching for the best possible transformation.
- **A developer can hint at stable identity across renders with `key`.** Rather than solving the general "which sequence of items best matches which" problem, the algorithm just trusts the key.

The trade-off is explicit: these heuristics are occasionally wrong (the type-swap case from the earlier slide, or a badly-chosen key), but they're right often enough, and cheap enough to run every render, that the occasional manual workaround is a better deal than an always-correct but far slower algorithm.

slides.sectionTitle: Debugging "state landed on the wrong row"
slides.markdown:
This is one of the most commonly asked practical debugging questions in this area, and a strong answer moves through cause to fix in order:

1. **Recognize the symptom**: a component's own internal state (expanded, editing, a local input value) appears attached to the wrong item after the list changed shape — insert, delete, filter, or sort.
2. **Name the cause**: the list is keyed by array index (or has no key at all), so the framework matches old and new items by position rather than identity, and reuses a component instance — state included — for what is now different data.
3. **Fix it**: key by a stable, unique identifier from the data itself, never the index or a randomly-generated value recomputed each render (which defeats the purpose just as badly, by never matching anything as "the same" at all).
4. **Generalize**: the same principle applies beyond `<li>` elements — any conditionally-rendered component swap (`{cond ? <A/> : <B/>}`) that should reset state relies on this exact type-mismatch behavior, and any swap that should *preserve* state across a condition change needs the same component type with different props instead.

Naming both the mechanism and the general principle — not just "add a key" — is what separates a memorized fix from real understanding.
